frameworks.name: Business Constraint Diagnosis
frameworks.definition: Systematically distinguish perceived constraints (intellectual curiosity, emotional preferences) from real ones (customer demand, unit economics, time leverage).

frameworks.name: Niching Decision Matrix
frameworks.definition: Niche down when operational efficiency improves through narrower delivery; expand avatar when back-end mechanics are identical but messaging differs.

claims.text: Between $1M–$3M revenue, most service businesses encounter the pressure to narrow their avatar and specialize their products because they have become good at multiple things simultaneously.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: A business's job is to serve customers, not to satisfy the owner's emotional needs or intellectual curiosity. If the service changed daily to match the founder's interests, it would create a terrible experience for customers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Inconsistent service offering (changing daily per founder mood) damages customer experience and trust.

claims.text: For a plastic surgery consulting business, the most profitable and repeatable service is medical staffing and HR (the least exciting), not the high-level consulting work.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: services: startup support, business assessments, ongoing consulting
claims.mechanism: Staffing is needed universally, takes less high-level manpower, and is offered as ongoing recurring revenue; high-touch consulting is time-intensive and non-repeatable.
bounded_by: Does not apply to business models where customization is the primary value

claims.text: Existing plastic surgery practices report that their primary need is not more profit, but freedom from constant delivery work—they feel on a treadmill and need time, simplicity, and efficiency.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Understaffing by ~3 people creates a delivery bottleneck that founder misinterprets as a profit problem.

claims.text: A practice assessment service priced at $15k for 2 on-site days + 60 days of implementation can be restructured to $35k–$50k delivered remotely without on-site visits, because customers only care that the problem is solved, not the delivery method.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: customers think in terms of surgeries per unit of work
claims.mechanism: Customers perceive the value as '1 day of work saves me 20 days of time'—a surgical metric—independent of delivery method. Removing travel overhead and on-site cost preserves perceived value while improving unit economics.

claims.text: Scaling from 8 conferences per year to 24 conferences per year (one every other week) is achievable for the plastic surgery consultant through delivery model compression and pricing optimization.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: consultant currently speaks at 8 conferences annually
claims.mechanism: Removing on-site delivery requirement frees time previously spent traveling + on-site assessment; pricing increase reflects compressed delivery model.
bounded_by: Limited by number of plastic surgery conferences that exist annually

claims.text: Niching down is important from an operational-efficiency perspective only when the nature of the work changes between avatars. When delivery mechanics are identical, expanding to multiple customer segments (e.g., plastic surgeons + med spas) requires only messaging variation, not service restructuring.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: delivery mechanism (operations, staffing model) is identical across avatars
claims.mechanism: When back-end service design is the same, different avatars simply need different hooks and messaging—no operational overhead to support multiple acquisition channels.
bounded_by: Does not apply when different avatars require different delivery models or service structures

claims.text: If a business owner's core service generates both the highest profit margin and the highest customer demand, that service should become the primary business, regardless of whether it feels intellectually interesting to the founder.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: one service dominates both profit and customer need metrics
claims.mechanism: The market reveals true value through willingness-to-pay and demand volume; founder emotion is a poor signal for business allocation.
bounded_by: May not apply to strategic positioning early in business growth where brand diversification is intentional

examples.text: A plastic surgery consultant charges $15k for a 2-day on-site assessment plus 60 days of implementation support, acquiring 1–2 practices per month through conferences (8 per year) and word-of-mouth referrals. The consultant observed that startups especially lack in-house management for HR and hiring—the service that generates the highest margin and is most repeatable—yet hesitates to make it the primary offering because HR and staffing feel boring compared to high-touch consulting work.

When asked what plastic surgery practices actually need, the consultant discovered that most do not seek higher profits—they seek relief from daily operational treadmill work. They want simplicity and efficiency. Upon inspection, their perceived problem (lack of profit) masks a real constraint: they are understaffed by approximately 3 people, creating a delivery bottleneck. The consultant's current solution (staffing/HR services) directly addresses this, yet staffing is not positioned as the primary offering.

practices.text: Boring businesses make the most money. Prioritize repeatable, unglamorous service lines over intellectually interesting ones when unit economics and customer demand support that choice.
Calculate the economic value of your time per activity (revenue per hour) and direct all activities below your target hourly rate to delegation or elimination, freeing time for high-value activities.

When pricing a service, frame the customer's value perception in terms they already use internally (e.g., surgeries per unit of work). Show that 1 unit of your time = many multiples of their recovered time.
